title: Saveloy with chips
subtitle: British chip-shop saveloy with twice-cooked chips
excerpt: The bright-red, spiced pork saveloy sausage, steamed until skin-tight and bursting, served in the British chip-shop tradition alongside thick twice-fried chips and a splash of chip-shop vinegar.
sourceNotes: The saveloy is a British and Irish street food staple with origins in the continental cervelas sausage, which appears in British food writing from the nineteenth century. The chip-shop saveloy is documented across British food history texts including Dorothy Hartley's Food in England (1954) and in numerous British culinary surveys of the post-war era. The chip-shop serving tradition is a distinctively British institution.

glossaryTerms.definition: A British pre-cooked, smoked, or cured pork sausage with a vivid red skin, sold in chip shops, street food stalls, and butchers. It is fully cooked when bought and only needs to be heated through. The skin is characteristic: tight, slightly shiny, and deep crimson.

content.text: is a chip-shop constant in London, South East England, and the Midlands. It is not a cooking sausage: it is pre-cooked and only needs gentle heating in water, ideally until the skin is taut enough to snap when bitten. Served at the chip-shop counter with a portion of chips and a splash of spirit vinegar, it is one of the more satisfying things you can eat on a cold evening.

items.prepNote: bought from a butcher or chip shop supplier
floury variety, peeled and cut into thick chips (2 cm)

content.text: Rinse the {{potato}} of cut chips in cold water until the water runs clear. Dry very thoroughly. Heat the oil to 140°C in a large, deep, heavy pan. Fry the chips in batches for 8 to 10 minutes until cooked through but pale. Drain on kitchen paper and cool.
Heat the saveloys and second-fry the chips

Bring a saucepan of water to a bare simmer, about 80°C. Add the saveloys. Heat for 10 to 15 minutes until the skins are tight and the sausages are hot through. Do not boil: a vigorous boil will burst the skins and the saveloys will lose their colour and texture.
Raise the chip oil to 190°C. Fry the chips in batches for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and season with salt.
Serve the saveloys alongside the chips with malt vinegar and, if you like, ketchup.

items.fix: Keep the water below 90°C. The saveloy just needs to be hot through, not boiled.

items.cause: Oil not hot enough for the second fry
items.fix: Wait for the oil to fully recover to 190°C between batches.

content.text: The saveloy is predominantly a south of England and Midlands chip-shop food. In London, particularly the East End, it is a long-established street food staple: as much a part of the chip-shop counter as the cod and the mushy peas. Outside London and the South East, the saveloy is less common; in the North and Scotland, the red pudding and the white pudding take its place. The saveloy with chips is the kind of meal that announces itself through a paper cone, eaten standing up, with vinegar soaking through to the chips at the bottom.
